stories.title: Legal aid changes 'unfair, illogical', High Court finds
stories.summary: The High Court has found that new regulations brought in by Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan to govern the payment of legal aid in criminal cases are "grossly unfair" and "demonstrably illogical". The new regulations providing for a flat fee of €520 to be paid per accused person, regardless of the number of charges against them or the number of court appearances, are at the centre of a dispute between the minister and criminal legal aid solicitors which has disrupted the criminal justice system for more than four months. Solicitor John Quinn challenged the new regulations in a judicial review. Mr Quinn, and the solicitors' representative body, the Law Society, who were notice parties to the case, argued the new regulations were unlawful as they provided for the certification and payment of legal aid in a way that went beyond the legislation. In her ruling, Ms Justice Mary Rose Gearty said the provision in the new scheme of a single payment to a solicitor when the final order in the case is made is "grossly unfair". The minister has since tweaked the scheme, allowing for two-thirds of the fee to be paid at the beginning of the case and the remainder at the end of the case or after 12 months.

stories.title: Phrase 'easy money' on Telly Bingo 'misleading'
stories.summary: National Lottery sales amounted to €871.6 million in 2025 - an increase of €16 million last year, compared to 2024. That's according to the annual report released by the Office of the Regulator of the National Lottery, Carol Boate. Over a quarter (27%) of all sales in 2025 - or €240.8 million - was transferred to the Exchequer to the Good Causes fund, while 58% or €504.4 million were won in prizes. In the report the Regulator's Office detailed its oversight, reforms, and player protection measures implemented over the last year. The review of National Lottery's online marketing led to increasing the group of at-risk players with possible gambling issues, to whom marketing emails are disabled for a longer period. Following a complaint the review found phrases "easy money" and "giving away lots of cash" used during the show.

stories.title: What you need to know about the 2026 US midterm elections
stories.summary: Early voting has been under way for weeks ahead of the midterm elections, when US voters will elect members of the House of Representatives and Senate and governors in states across the country. Held in the middle of each four-year presidential term, the midterms by definition do not involve the president. However, for anyone who thinks they lack drama or importance this year, consider these two statistics: More than 57 million people had already cast their ballots as of Monday, according to the University of Florida Election Lab, well above the 46 million who voted early in the 2022 midterm elections. This election is on track to be the most expensive in US history. The nonpartisan watchdog OpenSecrets estimates a total of $11.9 billion will be spent by candidates and outside political groups. Elon Musk alone had spent about $366 million to support Republicans as of three weeks ago, according to campaign finance records.

stories.title: Cunha sees red but caps quickfire comeback win over Roma
stories.summary: Matheus Cunha's late brace secured Manchester United a jaw-dropping 3-2 comeback win against Roma to breathe new life into their season and ease some of the pressure on Michael Carrick. A nine-match winless run had left the Red Devils head coach’s job hanging by a thread and Tuesday’s wretched start in the Champions League only pushed him closer to the Old Trafford exit. United were facing a fourth straight loss after Matias Soule’s avoidable opener was followed up by a Donyell Malen penalty in a first half that ended with boos. Green and gold balloons had cascaded down the Stretford End as fans protested against the Glazers before the match, with the second half offering a reminder of the special spirit that underpins their club. Bruno Fernandes pulled one back from a retaken, and softly awarded, second-half spot-kick as United played with the kind of purpose and skill lacking this term. That approach forced a late error that Cunha capitalised on, before the Brazil forward slammed in off the inside of the near post for the winner.

stories.title: KIDS Book Club: Travel back in time with historical fiction
stories.summary: As 2026 comes to a close and we look towards the near future of 2027, there are so many technological advances, social changes and big moments that have shaped and shifted our world this year. While we certainly can't predict the future, there is one way we can revisit our past and it doesn’t involve inventing a time machine! Historical fiction is a fantastic way to travel through time and experience how the world has changed in a unique way. For better or worse, we can see how technology has changed, remember interesting historical figures, see the progress of Ireland or even experience the discovery of new world cultures. History buffs, this month’s book club is for you – enjoy travelling through time with some fantastic stories. The Flying Feminist by Mary Boone, illustrated by Andrea Turk, Andersen Press, 32PP ISBN 9781839135101 This picturebook is based on the true story of the amazing Lilian Bland, the first woman to design, build and even fly her own airplane in 1910. Lilian’s story is one of bravery, tenacity, and the absolute refusal to give up on herself, even when everyone else had.

stories.title: Andrew Scott-starring Elsinore leads BIFA nominations
stories.summary: The Andrew Scott-starring Elsinore leads the shortlist for this year's British Independent Film Awards (BIFA) with 12 nominations. stories.title: West Cork couple tie the knot in surprise wedding on US chat show
stories.summary: Most couple's nuptials are presided over by a parish priest or maybe even a close friend or relative, but for one West Cork couple, theirs was led by none other than an Oscar-winning star. Amanda Murnane and Brendan Hayes, a couple from Bantry, became the first couple to wed on The Jennifer Hudson Show last month, in a surprise ceremony that was officiated by the bubbly host herself. The couple have a long love story, having been together for 27 years and sharing three children, Rene, Clarice and Michael, and one grandson, Wayne. Both have spent years working for West Cork Mental Health Services, while Brendan is also an independent filmmaker, documentary maker, writer, actor and director. Although they had long wanted to get married, a number of obstacles held them back, most notably in 2011 when their daughter Rene was diagnosed with leukemia. While Rene eventually overcame that health setback, that period of their lives was marked by stress and difficulty, which led Brendan to wanting to give Amanda something positive. Their story got another cinematic twist on 23 October when Brendan surprised Amanda with an elaborately planned wedding on stage, in front of a live studio audience. The plan was hatched over months, with Brendan secretly arranging the surprise alongside the show's production team.

stories.title: PSNI arrest man in Carrie Mullane murder investigation
stories.summary: PSNI detectives investigating the disappearance of Carrie Mullane (Noonan) have launched a murder investigation and arrested a man on suspicion of murder. 39-year-old Ms Mullane, from Limerick, is known to have travelled to Enniskillen, Co Fermanagh on 10 October. Since then, there have been no confirmed sightings of her, nor has she been in touch with her family or friends. Detective Superintendent Richard Thornton from the PSNI's Serious Crime Branch, said it is "extremely out of character" for Ms Mullane to not contact her loved ones, which has led to grave concerns for her safety. "Family and friends of Carrie tell us that she is usually in almost daily contact with them and not hearing from her has caused them to fear something may have happened to her after she reached Northern Ireland," Mr Thornton said. Ms Mullane arrived in Enniskillen by bus on Saturday 10 October, travelling with a man known to her, and from the bus depot on Wellington Road she and her companion then took a taxi at around to an address in Trasna Park.

stories.title: Apple forecasts margin drop as rising memory costs bite
stories.summary: Apple has warned that the cost of memory chips would continue to rise, pressuring gross margin for the crucial Christmas quarter, but said it had taken steps to lock in supplies. Shares, little changed in after-hours trading after fiscal fourth-quarter results beat expectations, fell 4% during a conference call after executives outlined the weaker outlook, but later pared losses to a 2% decline. Early demand for the iPhone 18 Pro lineup and higher prices boosted the quarter. Apple said it expects gross margin of 45% to 46% in the quarter ending in December, down from 47.9% in the fourth quarter. It forecast services revenue growth of 8% to 9%, below analysts' expectations of 10.7%. The results come as Apple experiments with a string of firsts under new CEO John Ternus, who took over in September. After nearly two decades of launching most new iPhones each autumn, Apple this year is spacing them out, with iPhone Pro and Duo models shipping this year and other models expected next year. Apple also released a bevy of new non-iPhone products this quarter, including its first touchscreen laptops and first smart-home hub. The steady drumbeat of releases, analysts said, is meant to smooth out Apple's yearly revenue cycle, which for decades showed a huge holiday-quarter boom that petered out by late summer.

stories.title: Raphinha rampant as Barcelona overwhelm Aston Villa
stories.summary: Barcelona ensured Unai Emery had another Nou Camp nightmare as they beat his Aston Villa side 3-0 in the Champions League. Lamine Yamal's early opener and a second-half double for Europe’s most prolific scorer Raphinha, who has bagged 19 in 13 games this season, gave Emery a 55th birthday to forget. The Spaniard will not be keen to return to this city any time soon as he has now lost 15 out of 16 matches at Barca, including the famous 'Remontada’ nine years ago, when his PSG side lost a last-16 tie 6-1 to squander a 4-0 first-leg lead. This was supposed to be a Red Letter Day for the club – a reward for their excellent progress in the four years of Emery’s reign. It might have been more memorable had Villa taken a number of first-half chances to draw level, but defeat ends their 100% start to the league phase. But with some winnable games still to come, they are still a good bet to finish in the top eight.

stories.title: All you need to know about why Godzilla has endured for so long
stories.summary: Analysis: Cinema's greatest monster has been on the loose for 72 years and has been reimagined, reinvented and changed in dramatic ways during this period It's Godzilla Day, the annual celebration spearheaded by the Japanese film studio (and owners of the Godzilla film franchise) Toho. It's 72 years since the release of Ishiro Honda's original Godzilla film and Godzilla Day 2026 will see the release of the latest Godzilla film, Godzilla Minus Zero. The film is the 39th in the long-running franchise and reunites the titular monster with director Takashi Yamazaki, who previously helmed 2023’s Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One. Next year will see the release of Grant Sputore’s Godzilla Supernova, a continuation of the American Monsterverse series (think the Marvel Cinematic Universe, but swap out Captain America and Iron Man for Godzilla and King Kong). The Japanese Godzilla films are usually sorted into four main categories or 'eras’: the Showa era, the Heisei era, the Millennium era and the Reiwa era (the first, second and fourth eras refer to the reigns of successive Japanese emperors that overlap with release dates). In each era, the monster has found itself reimagined and reinvented, changing in dramatic ways. These reinventions are why Godzilla has endured so well – the monster is adaptable and is consistently used to respond to (or metaphorically depict) major historical and political events. Here are some of the notable roles Godzilla has served over the past seven decades. The very first Godzilla is a strange film. The monster now has a reputation as the star of entertainingly bizarre and often funny action films. Little of this exuberance is to be found in Ishiro Honda’s stark 1954 masterpiece, which is a bleak, fantastical reckoning with post-war life in 1950s Japan. Characters make casual, desultory reference to the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, while continuing atomic tests in the South Pacific hang over proceedings (Godzilla is implied to have been awoken by tests near Bikini Atoll). The 1954 case of the Lucky Dragon fishing vessel – where the crew suffered radiation poisoning, social alienation and death as a result of nuclear tests – served as an inspiration for both the monster and its victims. In one dark scene, after Godzilla has levelled Tokyo, scientists scan children at an abandoned school with a Geiger counter. They shake their heads in sadness as the results, offscreen, indicate severe poisoning.

stories.title: Wild Horse Nine: a quirky companion piece to In Bruges
stories.summary: We are back on an isolated island in the company of two men struggling to communicate with each other in the enigmatic and hugely entertaining new movie from Banshees of Inisherin writer and director Martin McDonagh. It’s another wonky bromance from the Anglo-Irish auteur, this time with John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell as two CIA agents working to undermine Salvador Allende’s government in Chile in 1973. When they take a trip to Easter Island, 3,500km out into the Pacific, it leads to a reckoning and a form of redemption for at least one of them among the island’s famous statues. It seems like the shaggiest of shaggy dog stories and things take time to fall into place in what is very genre fluid movie. It’s a twisty comedy caper, a well-timed critique of US foreign policy, and a political thriller with all the twitchy paranoia of early seventies movie-making. They might as well give Malkovich the Oscar right now. He plays Chris Carlisle, an eccentric and melancholic CIA operative who is riddled with both terminal cancer and Catholic guilt over his very amoral life. He claims his dying wish is to see those monolithic statues, staring blankly out to the mighty ocean and perhaps he sees a form of salvation in the stony sentinels. His partner is Lee Chesterfield, played by McDonagh regular Sam Rockwell, and he has his own reasons for tagging along for the ride. This odd couple spend most of the time driving around in a battered old coupe (the coup comes later), bickering as they take in the sights and discuss the nature of the dirty work they carry out on behalf of the US government with all the exacting efficiency of accountants. Chris is also seeking to salve his conscious after a lifetime of murder and mayhem by writing his tell-all memoirs. As he says to Lee at one point, "I’ve killed people in countries you can’t even spell." He spends his nights recording notes into a Dictaphone, listening to Hank Williams, taking morphine, and worrying about the moths who circle about his hotel bedroom. After a life of covert operations and plausible deniability, he is now in the business of carefree confession.

stories.title: 8 household jobs to tackle in November
stories.summary: Although it might feel too early to put up your Christmas tree, there are plenty of cleaning jobs to tick off this November before the festivities start to ramp up. Here are eight household chores to tackle now during the quieter season before the fast-approaching holiday rush begins… It’s common to forget about the freezer until you are confronted with overflowing shelves of mystery food just before Christmas. "Go into the freezer and have a proper clear-out before all the Christmas food starts to arrive," recommends cleaning and organising expert and Sunday Times bestselling author Gemma Bray, also known as The Organised Mum. She suggests getting creative with your meal planning to clear out as much freezer food as possible before Christmas. "This will help you save money [on food] that you can repurpose towards your Christmas budget, and will also free up room in the freezer for all of the festive goodies that will come in," explains Bray.

stories.summary: Spain's transport minister, Oscar Puente, has announced his resignation over last week's deadly train crash, the country's second this year, hours after laying out the government's emergency aid package for victims and new safety measures. "A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot continue in office with two accidents of this severity in less than a year," he told lawmakers of the Permanent Deputation, a standing committee that sits when parliament is dissolved. He spoke nearly a week after the 28 October crash that killed 69 people near the town of Urda in central Spain. His departure comes less than four weeks before an early parliamentary election that Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez calledfor 29 November, and after two deadly crashes on the same line this ‌year. Mr Sanchez praised Mr Puente in a post on ⁠X, thanking him for his work and saying the minister had put victims first and acted out of a sense of political responsibility. Mr Puente, who had previously ruled out resigning, said he had decided to step down within minutes of learning of the crash, but chose to remain in office until the immediate emergency response was under way, preliminary investigations had begun and the first measures to compensate victims and improve rail safety had been put in place.

stories.title: Primark-Penneys owner forecasts further profit decline
stories.summary: Associated British Foods has today forecast another year of lower profits after reporting a 14% fall in earnings for 2025/26, pressured by deepening losses in its sugar business and lower underlying sales at its Primark/Penneys fashion chain. The FTSE 100 group, which plans to demerge Primark from its food businesses next year, said it remained cautious on consumer sentiment as well as the impact of inflation and higher energy costs on its businesses. It said adjusted operating profit in the year to September 2027 would be below the £1.51 billion reported in 2025/26, largely due to sugar losses that could widen to as much as £170m. "Any consumer facing business is trading with the reality of consumers whose spending power is reduced," CEO George Weston told Reuters. Shares in the group were down 3.1%, extending losses this year to 11.5%. AB Foods said work on the demerger was progressing well and remained on track for completion in December 2027.

stories.title: McNamara appointment 'great news' for Leinster - Keenan
stories.summary: Leinster full-back Hugo Keenan has hailed the "exciting appointment" of Noel McNamara as the province's next head coach. The Clare native, who spent five years at Leinster between 2016 and 2021 in a variety of development roles, will succeed Leo Cullen as head coach next summer. While McNamara has never been head coach at senior level, the 43-year-old spent two years as head coach of Ireland's Under-20 team between 2019 and 2021, while he has most recently helped Bordeaux-Begles to successive Investec Champions Cup titles. "I think it's great news, I've got a good relationship with him," Keenan said of this morning's announcement. "I would have worked with him in the past, both at UCD originally, he was the head coach there when I was playing AIL, when I was sort of between the Academy and Sevens and playing AIL rugby, and then dealt with them as well for the 'A' team in Leinster, and know him well. "Obviously that was a couple of years ago, and he's progressed so well since.

stories.title: Mourners told Mageean was an 'inspirational human being'
stories.summary: Mourners at the funeral of Irish Olympian and European champion Ciara Mageean have been told she was a bright light in the darkness who made the world a nicer place to call home. Hundreds of people packed into St Patrick's Church, just a few hundred metres along the road from her home in Portaferry in Co Down, with many more standing outside. There was a guard of honour by members of her local Portaferry GAA club, where she took her first sporting steps playing camogie. President Catherine Connolly and Taoiseach Micheál Martin were represented by their aides-de-camp, and Sinn Féin deputy leader and Northern Ireland’s First Minister Michelle O’Neill attended the service. Well known figures from the world of sport, including Irish Olympians and GAA President Jarlath Burns were also present. Many others watched a livestream of the service from across the world.

stories.title: Champions Lge round-up: Bayern tame Atleti, PSG run riot
stories.summary: Paris Saint-Germain produced another stunning Champions League display in a 6-0 rout of Villarreal to move three points clear at the top of the table. Harry Kane missed out on equalling Cristiano Ronaldo’s record of scoring in 11 consecutive Champions League matches in Bayern Munich’s 2-0 win at Atletico Madrid. PSG delivered another statement win in as Fabian Ruiz struck twice in Spain as Villarreal were the latest side to be put to the sword. Luis Enrique’s side, who made it 10 straight wins, were 4-0 up inside 17 minutes, with Joao Neves, Desire Doue, Senny Mayulu and Ruiz all on target. Ruiz put PSG 5-0 up early in the second half and substitute David Boly completed the scoring in the 78th minute. England skipper Kane, appearing in his first European tie since winning the Ballon d’Or, had scored in his previous 10 Champions League appearances, but drew a rare blank as second-half goals from teenager Lennart Karl and Konrad Laimer sealed victory in Madrid.

stories.title: Two Ryanair flights from Dublin searched after bomb hoax
stories.summary: Four Ryanair flights were searched on Tuesday, including two that departed from Dublin airport, following potential bomb threats. Two Ryanair flights, one from Lisbon and one from Dublin, were searched in Rome's Fiumicino airport after separate bomb alerts. stories.title: Connolly: The pundits are backing Waterford to win it
stories.summary: Derry City interim-manager Mark Connolly says the majority of pundits are backing Waterford in Sunday's Club Orange Men's FAI Cup final but he's confident his team are entering the decider in a buoyant frame of mind on the back of a difficult year. The Candystripes endured an incredibly turbulent first half of the season, marred by the saga over James McClean's unhappy return to the club and their disastrous drop-off in form in the league. Connolly, a Cup winner with the club in 2022, had returned as Director of Football at the beginning of the season. When Tiernan Lynch was sacked as manager at the start of August, the 34-year old was installed as interim manager despite not possessing a UEFA Pro Licence. Notwithstanding the lack of paperwork, he has overseen a transformation in form at Derry. While their long-touted league ambitions were already shot to pieces, they finished the campaign in decent form and this has been accompanied by another surge in the Cup. They dispatched Dundalk 4-2 in the quarter-finals and it was after the 2-0 win away to Galway United in the semi-final, that Connolly fully believed that the club were back in tune with their supporters. "This season as a whole has been a difficult one," Connolly told reporters at Tuesday's press conference.

stories.title: Scarlett Faulkner struck with 'brutal force', trial told
stories.summary: A jury in the trial of a woman and teenage girl accused of murdering Scarlett Faulkner in Co Tipperary last March has been told she was "hunted down" and struck with "brutal and ferocious force" with a metal pole. The 28-year-old died on 13 April after an incident at Birdhill in Co Tipperary on 21 March last. In his opening statement, prosecuting counsel Seoirse Ó Dúnlaing said the two accused women had acted in a joint enterprise to find and harm Ms Faulkner after discovering she had begun a relationship with an ex-partner of the older accused. He told the jury it would hear evidence that the vehicle in which Ms Faulkner was travelling on 13 April had been rammed off the road at Birdhill before she was struck 10 to 11 times with a metal pole by the 17-year-old accused. He said dashcam and other mobile phone footage would show Ms Faulkner being hit with the metal bar by the younger accused before the older woman approached and brought her co-accused back to their vehicle. Mr Ó Dúnlaing said the jury would hear evidence that the older woman had begun looking for Ms Faulkner the previous night and had sent Ms Faulkner's sister a text message saying: "Your smell bag of a sister will pay for what she done when I get her I’ll draw a map of Ireland on her face."

stories.title: Championship wrap: Kenny injury blow, more Cullen minutes
stories.summary: Republic of Ireland international Johnny Kenny was forced off in the first half of Preston's 3-2 defeat to Sheffield United at Deepdale after suffering a hamstring injury. The former Sligo Rovers and Shamrock Rovers striker was chasing down a long pass forward when he pulled up and eventually limped off in the 13th minute for the Championship strugglers. Kenny joined Preston from Celtic on a permanent deal on transfer deadline day and has since gone on to score two goals in eight Championship appearances. Meanwhile, fellows Boys in Green international Andrew Moran made his first league start of the season for Preston and played the full 90 minutes, while Sheffield United centre-forward Tom Cannon also featured for the entirety. Liam Kitching, who made his Ireland debut in September, missed out for the Blades due to a one-match suspension. Sydie Peck was the difference-maker in the game as he bagged a first-half hat-trick for Sheffield United. The 22-year-old inadvertently equalised with an intended cross in the 27th minute, put his team ahead with a gorgeous second from just outside the box 10 minutes later, and sealed his treble with a tap-in on the stroke of the interval.

stories.title: Patrick O'Donovan consulted on who would take portfolio
stories.summary: Patrick O'Donovan was involved in "consultations" over who would be selected to assume his portfolio, a spokesman for the Tánaiste has said. Taoiseach Micheál Martin agreed to a request from Tánaiste Simon Harris to allow  Enterprise Minister Peter Burke to take over the Media Minister's functions  during Mr O'Donovan's recovery from an illness. He became ill as he hosted EU telecommunications ministers at an event in Limerick last month. Mr O'Donovan, who is now a minister without portfolio, has spoken openly about being diagnosed with epilepsy and was treated at University Hospital Limerick. Today, a spokesman for Mr Harris refused to offer a potential date for Mr O'Donovan's return to his duties, adding it would be "guided by medical advice". Asked how Mr Burke was selected, the spokesman said a decision was taken "in consultation" with Mr O'Donovan and Mr Martin.

stories.title: McMenamin replaces McGee on Sligo management team
stories.summary: Three-time All-Ireland winner Ryan McMenamin has joined the Sligo management team for the 2027 season, replacing former Donegal defender Eamon McGee. McGee had been part of Dessie Sloyan and Eamonn O'Hara's backroom team for the 2026 campaign but was unable to commit for the upcoming year. McMenamin, a famed defender from Tyrone's golden era in the 2000s, previously managed Fermanagh from 2019 to 2021. On joining the Sligo coaching ticket, he links up with his former inter-county team-mate Joe McMahon, with whom he won All-Ireland titles as a player in 2005 and 2008. There has already been change to the Sligo management team for the 2027 season, with the joint-managerial arrangement between Sloyan and O'Hara being tweaked, the former taking the role of manager and the latter being named as assistant manager. Sligo had a disappointing season in 2026, losing at home to Leitrim in the Connacht championship for the first time in 15 years and being heavily beaten by Fermanagh in the Tailteann Cup quarter-final. They did, however, retain their Division 3 status amid a difficult year.

stories.title: Trump says US ending $4 billion in annual aid for Israel
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump has said he had made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Washington would stop $4 billion in annual funding to Israel after this year, but will still sell weapons to its close Middle East ally. In a surprise announcement as US voters headed to the polls for midterm elections, he cast the move as partly meant to take away a "bad talking point" he said left-wing Democrats had used against Republicans over support for military assistance to Israel. Mr Trump did not provide details or explain how the funding would be halted at the end of the year, given that the memorandum of understanding that provides $3.8 billion in US military aid to Israel each year does not expire until September 2028. However, he seemed to acknowledge that aid to Israel, no longer the solid source of bipartisan consensus it had been for decades, had become a political liability for him among some voters. Analysts suggested his declaration was timed as an election day ploy. Discussions have been under way on how US assistance to Israel would evolve beyond 2028, and Mr Netanyahu had already said he expects US aid to wind down over time.

stories.title: People on hospital trolleys up 12% since 2025 - govt memo
stories.summary: The number of people on hospital trolleys during morning counts has increased by at least 12% since last year, Cabinet has been told. The figure is included in an Urgent And Emergency Care update briefing provided to ministers by Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill, and which has called on the HSE to outline an emergency unit winter plan for each health service region. Between 1 January and 28 October, the number of people on hospital trolleys as of 8am every morning was 12% higher than the previous year - with targets failing to be met on 61% of days, according to the Cabinet briefing. In addition, the number of people admitted to emergency departments was up 7% or 98,300 people, and up 9% or 17,700 people among those aged 75 or older. The Cabinet file also said "delayed transfers of care" remain one of the most significant factors in hospital overcrowding, with 516 people seeing their departure from hospital delayed every day compared to a target of 300 - resulting in more than 150,000 lost bed days so far this year. As part of attempts to address the situation, the Department of Health has asked the HSE to put in place "co-ordinated and focused" approaches to winter planning over the coming months in all health service regions.

stories.title: Former Israeli generals condemn West Bank settler attacks
stories.summary: A group of senior Israeli ex-military officials helped Palestinian farmers to harvest olives, in a gesture of solidarity amid an upsurge in militant settler violence targeting Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. "When I see what is going on here, when I see these guys come... and hit women and kids, it reminds me of stories from my parents from the time when the Jewish people suffered," said former major general Eyal Ben-Reuven, who compared the militant settler attacks to pogroms. Mr Ben-Reuven said he began organising a group of around 30 senior military officials -including six generals - several months ago following an increase in settler violence that many Palestinians say is enabled by the Israeli military. The Israeli military has said it condemns violence and it operates to maintain security in the West Bank. "Occupation is the main problem of Israeli society. I believe we must deal with it, we cannot ignore it. We must try to solve it together with the Palestinians," former colonel Doron Meinert said. Mr Ben-Reuven and others said they were also concerned about the impact of settler violence on Israel's global reputation.

stories.title: US votes in midterms that could reshape Trump presidency
stories.summary: Millions of Americans have voted in a midterm election seen as a referendum on Donald Trump that could wrest control of Congress from Republicans and impose major restraints on the president's remaining two years in office. Polls predict the Democrats will win a majority in the House of Representatives and possibly seize the Senate on the back of voter resentment at an unpopular president, soaring energy costs and the ongoing conflict with Iran. Republicans losing the House would give Democrats the power to stall Mr Trump's legislative agenda and launch sweeping investigations of his administration. A Senate defeat would threaten his ability to appoint Supreme Court justices and senior officials - and signal that Mr Trump's overwhelming dominance of US politics is finally fading. Mr Trump, 80, defended his record in a final TV phone-in pitch to voters, saying he had rebuilt the country through his immigration crackdown, war on Iran and tariffs. "We have to keep America great. We're great now. We were terrible two years ago," Mr Trump told Fox News.

stories.title: Tenerife's Jesus De Miguel dies after on-field collision
stories.summary: Tenerife player Jesus De Miguel has died after an on-field collision in a match on Monday, his club have announced. The collision occurred as Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono raced from his goal to challenge 30-year-old striker De Miguel for the ball in stoppage time of a Spanish second tier game. The Canary Islands club said in a statement on Tuesday: "Racked with pain, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe that this is true, from CD Tenerife we communicate the tragic passing, this Tuesday, November 3, 2026, at 8:00 a.m., of Jesus de Miguel Alameda. "There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this feeling overflowing with sadness. "We stand alongside his devastated family, alongside his loved ones…that today weep for this cruel outcome. The family of Jesus de Miguel thanks each and every one of the expressions of support received, and likewise requests, from the heart, the utmost respect for their privacy in these terrible moments." Late on Monday night Tenerife issued a statement confirming De Miguel had been admitted to hospital and was initially described as "stable despite the severity of his condition".

stories.title: Leinster confirm McNamara appointment as Cullen successor
stories.summary: Leinster have confirmed the appointment of Noel McNamara as head coach to succeed Leo Cullen when he departs his role at the conclusion of the 2026/27 season. McNamara will join Leinster from Union Bourdeaux-Begles where he is currently the club's attack coach, helping them to deliver back-to-back European Champions Cup titles. The Clare native will be returning to the Irish province having previously worked with the club in several roles, including academy manager and Leinster 'A’ head coach during a five-year spell between 2016 and 2021. He also coached the Ireland Under 20s to a Grand Slam in 2019 before spending two years in Durban with the Sharks as their attack and backs coach prior to joining Bordeaux. McNamara will remain in his position with Bordeaux for the remainder of the 2026/27 season before taking up his new role with Leinster on 1 July 2027. "I am delighted that I am returning to Leinster Rugby as head coach in 2027," McNamara said. "This is one of the most prestigious roles in world rugby and it is an honour to be given this responsibility.
